question.text: You can copy a computer file perfectly, a billion times. Why can't a quantum computer copy a qubit even once?
options: Qubits are physically too small for any read head to grab onto
Reading an unknown quantum state disturbs it — and you can't copy what you can't fully read
Copying a qubit would transmit information faster than light
Quantum computers don't have enough memory to hold two copies
question.hint: The problem isn't the copying. It's the looking.

explain.g: The no-cloning theorem. To copy something you first have to read it — but measuring a qubit collapses its superposition, destroying the very information you wanted to copy. You can't look without disturbing, and you can't copy what you can't look at.
explain.y: A universal copier would need to duplicate a state it doesn't know. Measurement only extracts one bit from a qubit's continuous (α, β) amplitudes and wrecks the rest. This is exactly why quantum error correction can't just keep backups — and why decoders (including AI ones like AlphaQubit) read indirect syndrome measurements instead of the data qubits themselves.
explain.r: Suppose a unitary U clones arbitrary states: U|ψ⟩|0⟩ = |ψ⟩|ψ⟩. For |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩+β|1⟩, linearity gives U|ψ⟩|0⟩ = α U|0⟩|0⟩ + β U|1⟩|0⟩ = α|00⟩ + β|11⟩. But cloning demands |ψ⟩|ψ⟩ = α²|00⟩ + αβ|01⟩ + αβ|10⟩ + β²|11⟩. Equal only when αβ = 0 — the basis states themselves. No universal cloner exists (Wootters & Zurek, Nature 299, 802 (1982); Dieks, Phys. Lett. A 92, 271 (1982)).
